system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 15 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2170-04-11 17:56:00 to 2170-04-26 14:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman was admitted with severe bilateral lower extremity swelling, a 18-pound weight gain, and erythema on the left shin concerning for cellulitis. She was started on IV vancomycin for a 7-day course, with improvement in redness and leukocytosis. Diuresis was attempted with IV furosemide and a lasix drip, resulting in initial fluid loss but complicated by acute kidney injury (creatinine rising to 1.6) and hypokalemia with contraction alkalosis. Diuresis was discontinued, and she was transitioned back to home oral diuretics. Echocardiogram showed normal heart function, and lower extremity ultrasound ruled out deep vein thrombosis. Her swelling improved with conservative measures including ACE wraps. She was discharged home with home health services, instructions to monitor weight, and follow-up for lab monitoring and lymphedema evaluation.
problems: Cellulitis and abscess of leg, except foot
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  CHEST (PORTABLE AP)

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with chronic lymphedema presents with weight
gain, dyspnea on exertion.  // Evaluate for pulmonary vascular congestion

TECHNIQUE:  CHEST (PORTABLE AP)

COMPARISON:  ___

IMPRESSION: 

Heart size and mediastinum are unremarkable. Lungs are essentially clear.
There is no pleural effusion or pneumothorax. There is no evidence of
pulmonary edema.

INDICATION:  New right PICC. Evaluate placement.

TECHNIQUE:  Single upright AP view of the chest.

COMPARISON:  Chest radiograph from ___.

FINDINGS: 

Since the prior exam, a new right PICC has been placed. It courses into the
right internal jugular vein.  The tip is out of the field of view.  The lungs
are clear without consolidation or edema. There is no pleural effusion or
pneumothorax. The cardiomediastinal silhouette is normal.

IMPRESSION: 

Right PICC extending into the right internal jugular vein.

NOTIFICATION:   The findings were discussed by Dr. ___ with ___ of the IV
team on the telephone on ___ at 1:07 ___, 1 minutes after discovery of
the findings.

INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with malpositioned PICC this AM. // Would like
PICC to be repositioned.

COMPARISON:  X-ray from the same day

TECHNIQUE:   OPERATORS: Dr. ___ resident) and Dr. ___
___ radiology attending) performed the procedure. The attending,
Dr. ___ was present and supervising throughout the procedure. Dr. ___,
___ radiologist, personally supervised the trainee during the key
components of the procedure and reviewed and agreed with the trainee's
findings.
ANESTHESIA: None
MEDICATIONS: None
CONTRAST: 0 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE: 1 min, 16 mGy

PROCEDURE:  1. Repositioning of right PICC.
PROCEDURE DETAILS: Using sterile technique and local anesthesia, the existing
PICC line was aspirated and flushed and a Nitinol guidewire was introduced
into the superior vena cava (SVC). A peel-away sheath was then placed over a
guidewire. The guidewire was then advanced into the superior vena cava. The
PICC was then withdrawn and replaced into the distal SVC under fluoroscopic
guidance. Position of the catheter was confirmed by a fluoroscopic spot film
of the chest. The peel-away sheath and guidewire were then removed. The
catheter was secured to the skin, flushed, and a sterile dressing applied.
The patient tolerated the procedure well. There were no immediate
complications.

FINDINGS: 

1. Existing right arm approach PICC with tip in the internal jugular
repositioned to the distal SVC

IMPRESSION: 

Successful repositioning of an existing right sided PICC, now in the distal
SVC

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You're here because your legs have been swelling more than usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ve gotten so big and painful. I’ve gained over 20 pounds in a few weeks. My legs are tight, they blister, and when I lie down, the swelling goes into my belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve been taking your diuretics, the water pills, like usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, every day. I’m also on salt and fluid limits. Nothing’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. We’ll start IV diuretics to help pull off the extra fluid. We’ll monitor your labs closely. Your heart function will be checked with an echo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help me breathe better? I get short of breath just walking to the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, reducing the fluid should help. The chest X-ray shows no fluid in your lungs now, so that’s good. But your legs are holding a lot of fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also had chills the last couple days. Could I be fighting an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your urine and it’s clean. No fever now, and no signs of cellulitis. We’ll keep you on doxycycline as a preventive since you’ve had it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re going to place a PICC line so we can give your IV diuretics safely over the next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I had a blood clot in my arm before from a PICC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand your concern. We’ll place it on the right side and confirm the position with an X-ray. We’ll also keep your warfarin going to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC is in, but the tip was too high. We’ll reposition it later today under X-ray guidance to make sure it’s in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get some numbing medicine. It’s a quick procedure, and you’ll be awake. Most patients tolerate it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC is now correctly placed in the large vein near your heart. We’ve started the IV lasix.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I already feel a little less pressure in my legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your echo came back. Your heart is pumping well, so this swelling isn’t from heart failure. It’s likely lymphedema or venous stasis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why am I so swollen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your body isn’t draining fluid properly, and with your weight, the veins and lymph system are under strain. The IV diuretics will help reduce the load.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. My weight hasn’t gone down much though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. The scale might not reflect changes if fluid shifts. But your legs do look smaller. We’re tracking your intake and output too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your white count is still high, but no infection signs. We’ll keep the doxycycline as a preventive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from stress or inflammation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely. Your body is under strain from the fluid overload. It’s not an infection, so we won’t add antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was low yesterday. We’ve increased your warfarin dose to 8 mg daily to get it back in range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on warfarin for years. Why is it fluctuating now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Illness, diet changes, or other meds can affect it. We’ll monitor closely and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m told you had a seizure last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember it. The nurse said I was twitching and frothing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looked like a generalized seizure. Your levetiracetam level was normal, but we think fluid overload may have triggered it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my level was okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but sometimes even therapeutic levels aren’t enough during stress. We’re increasing your dose to 1500 mg twice daily to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine went up slightly, so we’re stopping the IV lasix. We don’t want to hurt your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the swelling might come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch to a higher dose of oral bumetanide—4 mg daily. You’ll also go to the diuretic clinic for occasional IV treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about peeing all the time. Is 4 mg once a day okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with once daily to see how you tolerate it. We can adjust if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your A1c came back at 6.4, which suggests prediabetes. We’ll monitor your sugars and encourage diet changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve always had borderline sugars. Should I see an endocrinologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Your PCP can follow this. Focus on low-sugar choices and monitoring weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your legs are still swollen, but less tender. The papules on your skin aren’t infected. We’ll keep the antifungal cream for itching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The canker sores on my tongue are bothering me. Any advice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re common with stress or vitamin changes. Rinse with warm salt water. They should heal in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning discharge in a couple days. Your INR is now 2.0, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I want to get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled follow-up with your PCP to check your levetiracetam level and INR. Call if your weight goes up more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the diuretic clinic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll contact you to reschedule. You may need IV diuretics every few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge weight is 156.1 kg. It hasn’t changed much, but your legs look better. The scale might not capture fluid shifts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I feel lighter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging tomorrow. You’ll go home with increased levetiracetam, warfarin, and bumetanide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep using oxycontin and morphine as needed. Also, we added stool softeners to prevent constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final labs look stable. Your potassium is good, and white count is still mildly high but not concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the swelling might come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might. That’s why we’re setting up the diuretic clinic and close follow-up. Watch your weight and symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home tomorrow. A nurse will call with instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’ll get you discharged by noon. Your final meds are ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Remember: weigh daily, take your meds, and follow up with your PCP and neurology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And the diuretic clinic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll call you. If swelling worsens before then, come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will take you to the lobby in 30 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m all packed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your warfarin is now 8 mg daily. Check your INR at the lab next week and fax it to your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep taking the levetiracetam twice a day. Neurology will see you in two months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—I take the bumetanide once a day, not twice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We lowered it to once daily to reduce frequent urination. Call if swelling returns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ride is here. Here’s your discharge summary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman was admitted for acute on chronic lower extremity edema worsened over several weeks, unresponsive to oral diuretics. She was started on IV furosemide via a PICC line after initial placement and repositioning confirmed by imaging. Echocardiogram showed preserved systolic function, supporting lymphedema or venous stasis as the cause. The hospital course was complicated by a generalized seizure, likely triggered by volume overload, prompting an increase in levetiracetam dose despite therapeutic levels. IV diuresis was stopped due to a slight rise in creatinine, and she was transitioned to higher-dose oral bumetanide. Her warfarin was uptitrated to achieve a therapeutic INR. Leukocytosis persisted without infection. She was discharged home with increased diuretic and seizure medication, instructions for weight monitoring, and follow-up in primary care, neurology, and an outpatient diuretic clinic.
